doc.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
title: Bill's influence, his record collection and the music at home
summary: Bill's 78s and Philly radio shaped him; his mother watched Welk and his father whistled Lester Young.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: We talked off-mic about the disparity in age, difference in age between you and Bill, 17 years, but he obviously had some influence in your musical development, if nothing else than finding the gig. Was there much contact, growing up with Bill, if we can go back and talk about him?
Not growing up, other than seeing him at the dinner table. It’s like I say. In the beginning, before I started playing, we didn’t really – he was my big brother.
But he was already playing horn when he was still home.
Oh yeah. He was already playing.
Was he playing records at home?

Yeah, and that was another thing that was a big influence. He had a great record collection, 78s. He had Charlie Parker, Fats Navarro, Dexter Gordon – people like that, and I used to listen to them. So that was a big influence, as well as Philly also had really great jazz radio stations. So, those two things.
It seems that music was emphasized in the house, since you said everyone had piano lessons. What were your parents listening to? What music did they play in the house, if at all?

That’s interesting. My mother used to watch t.v. She’d watch Lawrence Welk. She loved Lawrence Welk. I think my father – he never went out that much to listen to music. But he – I remember he used to come home sometimes, and he was always whistling this song. It used to drive me crazy until I moved to New York and discovered what it was. It was Jumpin’ with Symphony Sid, Lester Young. He was always whistling
that song. Like I say, he didn’t go out and hang out and listen, but I think he appreciated the music.
